{{Short description|Statistical test}}
{{Distinguish|White information matrix test}}
'''White test''' is a [[statistical test]] that establishes whether the [[variance]] of the [[errors and residuals in statistics|errors]] in a [[regression model]] is constant: that is for  [[homoskedasticity]].

This test, and an estimator for [[heteroscedasticity-consistent standard errors]], were proposed by [[Halbert White]] in 1980.<ref>{{cite journal
 |last=White |first=H. |author-link=Halbert White
 |year=1980
 |title=A Heteroskedasticity-Consistent Covariance Matrix Estimator and a Direct Test for Heteroskedasticity
 |journal=[[Econometrica]]
 |volume=48 |issue=4 |pages=817–838
 |mr=575027 | jstor = 1912934
|doi=10.2307/1912934 |citeseerx=10.1.1.11.7646 }}</ref> These methods have become widely used, making this paper one of the most cited articles in economics.<ref>{{cite journal
 |title=What Has Mattered to Economics since 1970
 |journal=Journal of Economic Perspectives
 |volume=20 |number=4 |year=2006 |pages=189–202
 |last1=Kim |first1=E.H.
 |last2=Morse |first2=A.
 |last3=Zingales |first3=L.
 |doi=10.1257/jep.20.4.189
 |url=https://www.nber.org/papers/w12526.pdf
|doi-access=free}}</ref>

In cases where the White test statistic is statistically significant, heteroskedasticity may not necessarily be the cause; instead the problem could be a specification error. In other words, the White test can be a test of heteroskedasticity or specification error or both. If no cross product terms are introduced in the White test procedure, then this is a test of pure heteroskedasticity.
If cross products are introduced in the model, then it is a test of both heteroskedasticity and specification bias.

== Testing constant variance ==
To test for constant variance one undertakes an auxiliary regression analysis: this regresses the squared residuals from the original regression model onto a set of [[regressor]]s that contain the original regressors along with their squares and cross-products.<ref>{{cite book |first=Marno |last=Verbeek| author-link = Marno Verbeek|title=A Guide to Modern Econometrics |publisher=Wiley |year=2008 |edition=Third |isbn=978-0-470-51769-7 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/guidetomoderneco0003verb/page/99 99]–100 |url=https://archive.org/details/guidetomoderneco0003verb |url-access=registration }}</ref> One then inspects the ''R''<sup>2</sup>. The [[Lagrange multiplier test|Lagrange multiplier (LM) test]] statistic is the product of the ''R''<sup>2</sup> value and sample size:
:<math>\text{LM} = n R^2 .</math>
This follows a [[chi-squared distribution]], with degrees of freedom equal to ''P''&nbsp;−&nbsp;1, where ''P'' is the number of estimated parameters (in the auxiliary regression).

The logic of the test is as follows. First, the squared residuals from the original model serve as a proxy for the variance of the error term at each observation. (The error term is assumed to have a mean of zero, and the [[variance]] of a zero-mean random variable is just the expectation of its square.) The independent variables in the auxiliary regression account for the possibility that the error variance depends on the values of the original regressors in some way (linear or quadratic). If the error term in the original model is in fact homoskedastic (has a constant variance) then the coefficients in the auxiliary regression (besides the constant) should be statistically indistinguishable from zero and the ''R''<sup>2</sup> should be “small". Conversely, a “large" ''R''<sup>2</sup> (scaled by the sample size so that it follows the chi-squared distribution) counts against the hypothesis of homoskedasticity.

An alternative to the White test is the [[Breusch–Pagan test]], where the Breusch-Pagan test is designed to detect only linear forms of heteroskedasticity. Under certain conditions and a modification of one of the tests, they can be found to be algebraically equivalent.<ref>{{cite journal|doi=10.1016/0165-1765(83)90085-X|title=A note on algebraic equivalence of White's test and a variation of the Godfrey/Breusch-Pagan test for heteroscedasticity|journal=Economics Letters|volume=13|issue=2–3|pages=197–200|year=1983|last1=Waldman|first1=Donald M.}}</ref>

If homoskedasticity is rejected one can use [[heteroskedasticity-consistent standard errors]].

== Software implementations ==

* In [[R (programming language)|R]], White's Test can be implemented using the <code>white</code> function of the <code>skedastic</code> package.<ref>{{cite web|title=skedastic: Heteroskedasticity Diagnostics for Linear Regression Models|work=CRAN|url=https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/skedastic/index.html}}</ref>

* In [[Python (programming language)|Python]], White's Test can be implemented using the <code>het_white</code> function of the <code>statsmodels.stats.diagnostic.het_white</code> <ref>{{cite web|title=statsmodels v0.12.1|url=https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/generated/statsmodels.stats.diagnostic.het_white.html}}</ref>
*In [[Stata]], the test can be implemented using the <code>estat imtest, white</code> function.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Stata|date=|title=regress postestimation — Postestimation tools for regress|url=https://www.stata.com/manuals13/rregresspostestimation.pdf}}</ref>
